summary: At night before Caiaphas and the council, false witnesses fail, Jesus declares under oath that He is the Christ, and He is condemned as deserving death.
key_insight: As the guards blindfolded Jesus and jeered, “Prophesy!”, one of His prophecies was coming true in the courtyard below. Peter was denying Him, just as He had said he would.
story: Those who had arrested Jesus led Him to Caiaphas the high priest, {Mt} where all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes were assembled. {Mk} Peter followed at a distance, right into the high priest’s courtyard, and sat with the servants.

The chief priests and all the council looked for testimony against Jesus to put Him to death, but found none. Many bore false witness against Him, but their testimonies did not agree. {Mk} At last two came forward {Mt} and said, “We heard Him say, ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands.’ ” But not even then did their testimony agree. {Mk}
The high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, “Do You answer nothing? What is it these men testify against You?” But He kept silent and answered nothing. {Mk}

Then the high priest said, “I put You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God!” {Mt} Jesus said, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” {Mk}

The high priest tore his clothes. “He has spoken blasphemy! What further need do we have of witnesses? Look, now you have heard His blasphemy! What do you think?” {Mt} They all condemned Him to be deserving of death. {Mk}

Then some began to spit on Him, to blindfold Him and to beat Him. {Mk} They struck Him on the face and asked, “Prophesy! Who is the one who struck You?” {Lk} The officers struck Him with the palms of their hands, {Mk} and many other things they blasphemously spoke against Him. {Lk}
differences: Mark says the witnesses’ testimonies did not agree, even about the temple saying; Matthew says two false witnesses came forward at last.
In Matthew, Caiaphas puts Jesus under oath “by the living God” and asks if He is “the Christ, the Son of God.” In Mark he asks, “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”
Jesus’ answer: “I am” (Mark); “It is as you said” (Matthew).

Luke does not tell the night hearing. He says only that Jesus was brought into the high priest’s house and mocked by the men who held Him, and he records the council’s questions at daybreak (Luke 22:66–71).

fit.question: Did Jesus answer the high priest, “I am” (Mark) or “It is as you said” (Matthew)?

points.label: A Jewish way of saying yes
points.text: “It is as you said” is a firm yes that hands the words back to the questioner: you have said it, and it is true. Jesus answered Judas the same way that night: “You have said it” (Matthew 26:25).

points.label: Heard the same way
points.text: In both Gospels Jesus goes straight on to claim the right hand of the Power, and in both the high priest tears his clothes and calls it blasphemy. Mark gives the plain sense of the answer; Matthew keeps its form.

fit.note: The high priest’s reaction shows how the answer was understood. Both Gospels report a clear yes.
fit.short: “It is as you said” was a firm yes. Mark gives its plain sense, “I am”; the high priest heard it as a clear claim.

scene.label: A trial at night
scene.text: The full council had about seventy members. Jewish rules written down about AD 200 required capital trials to be held by day, with a guilty verdict given no sooner than the next day. Whether those rules were in force in Jesus’ time is uncertain, but this hearing was hurried and held in the dark.

scene.label: Two witnesses who agree
scene.text: The Law required two or three witnesses before anyone could be put to death (Deuteronomy 17:6), and a false witness was to suffer the penalty he intended for another (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). The council could not even find two who agreed.

scene.label: The temple saying
scene.text: Early in His ministry Jesus had said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), and John explains that He meant His body. The witnesses turned a dare into a threat: “I will destroy.”

scene.label: Psalm 110 and Daniel 7
scene.text: Jesus’ answer joins two Scriptures. In Psalm 110:1 the LORD says to David’s Lord, “Sit at My right hand.” In Daniel 7:13 One like the Son of Man comes “with the clouds of heaven” to receive a kingdom. “The Power” and “the Blessed” were reverent ways of saying God without speaking His name.

scene.label: Torn clothes
scene.text: Tearing one’s garments was the response to hearing God blasphemed. Hezekiah’s officials came to him with their clothes torn after the Assyrian envoy mocked the LORD (2 Kings 18:37; 19:6).

witnesses.matthew: Records the oath “by the living God,” so Jesus’ answer is sworn testimony. The mockers’ taunt, “Prophesy to us, Christ!”, throws back the very title the council had just rejected.
witnesses.mark: Stresses the failure of the witnesses: twice their testimony “did not agree.” Through much of Mark’s Gospel Jesus has told people to keep quiet about who He is; now, before the highest court in the land, He says plainly, “I am.”
witnesses.luke: Skips the night hearing and tells only the mockery while Jesus was held. He keeps the formal questions for the session at daybreak (22:66–71), separating what happened in the dark from the official meeting.

seeing.reveals: Silent before lies, Jesus speaks plainly when asked who He is. Bound and condemned, He tells His judges that they will see Him seated at God’s right hand and coming with the clouds.
seeing.living: Jesus did not defend Himself against false charges, but He would not deny the truth about Himself, even under oath and at the cost of His life. You may be wrongly accused and choose to stay quiet; you must never be quiet about who Jesus is.
seeing.ponder: The council judged Jesus that night; one day He will sit as Judge. How does knowing who will have the last word change the way you face being misjudged?

preaching.big_idea: On trial for His life, Jesus told the truth: the condemned Man is the coming Judge.
outline: A court that could not find the truth (53–59)
A silence that refused to argue (60–61a)
A confession that sealed the verdict (61b–64)
A mockery that missed the point (65)
preaching.watch_for: Follow the temple thread in Mark. The false witnesses accuse Jesus of threatening the temple (14:58); the mockers at the cross repeat the charge (15:29); and when Jesus dies, the veil of the temple is torn in two (15:38). The charge was false, but His death did change everything about the temple.
